explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The question asks who is wise enough to explain this, and then the LORD answers it Himself: “It is because they have forsaken My law…” (Jeremiah 9:13). No middleman and no guessing. The One whose mouth spoke gives the reason Himself.
I get the thinking, baker. Kings usually have plenty to say. But the text doesn't name a king anywhere in this answer. It says the LORD is the One who answers (Jeremiah 9:13).

A priest feels like a natural pick, friend. But no priest steps up in this passage. The LORD is the One who answers why the land is destroyed (Jeremiah 9:13), and He doesn't need anybody to explain it for Him.

explanations.answer: They forsook His law and did not obey His voice
explanations.explanation: Exactly, baker. The LORD says they have forsaken His law, which He set before them, and they have not walked in it or obeyed His voice (Jeremiah 9:13). The reason is right there in His own words. Nobody has to dig for it.

explanations.answer: They lost too many battles to their enemies
explanations.explanation: Battles do sound like the usual suspect for a ruined land, friend. But when the LORD gives His reason, He doesn't mention a single battle record. He says they forsook His law and did not obey His voice (Jeremiah 9:13).

explanations.answer: They let their fields go unplanted for years
explanations.explanation: Empty fields would make a scorched land make sense, baker. But the text never says anything about unplanted fields. The reason the LORD gives is that they forsook His law and did not obey His voice (Jeremiah 9:13).
That's the one, baker. The LORD says they followed the stubbornness of their hearts and “…gone after the Baals…” (Jeremiah 9:14). They didn't wander off by accident. They went after them.
Dagon isn't in this verse, friend. Here the LORD says they followed the stubbornness of their hearts and “…gone after the Baals…” (Jeremiah 9:14). The Baals are the name to hold onto.
The golden calf isn't in Jeremiah 9, baker. The LORD says they followed the stubbornness of their hearts and “…gone after the Baals…” (Jeremiah 9:14). That's the name to hold onto here.

I see why it might look that way, friend. But the LORD says they went after the Baals “…as their fathers taught them.” (Jeremiah 9:14). So someone did teach them. They weren't the first ones down that road.
Right, baker. The LORD says they went after the Baals “…as their fathers taught them.” (Jeremiah 9:14). It was handed down to them. That's a reminder that what we pass along matters.

explanations.answer: Among nations they have never known
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says He will scatter them “…among the nations that neither they nor their fathers have known…” (Jeremiah 9:16). Not just nations they hadn't met, but nations their fathers hadn't known either. That's a whole lot of unfamiliar ground.

explanations.answer: Among the cities of the Philistines
explanations.explanation: That's a specific guess, friend, but the LORD doesn't name the Philistines here. He says He will scatter them among nations that neither they nor their fathers have known (Jeremiah 9:16). Unfamiliar ground is the point.

Tents are a nice picture, baker, but Midian isn't named in this verse. The LORD says He will scatter them among nations that neither they nor their fathers have known (Jeremiah 9:16). Those are the nations to remember here.

That's right, baker. The LORD says the lament is so “…that our eyes may overflow with tears, and our eyelids may gush with water.” (Jeremiah 9:18). It's not a quiet sniffle. It's a full flood. This is a sad moment, and the text lets it be sad.
I wish that were the line, friend. But the text says nothing about enemies turning back. The lament is meant to bring tears: “…that our eyes may overflow with tears…” (Jeremiah 9:18).
Rain would be a gentle picture, baker, but the verse doesn't go there. The lament is for “…that our eyes may overflow with tears…” (Jeremiah 9:18). The water here comes from the eyes.

Yes, baker. The wailing from Zion says, “For we have abandoned the land because our dwellings have been torn down.” (Jeremiah 9:19). The homes are torn down and the people have left. I think that's a hard thing to say out loud.

This one is true, friend. The cry from Zion is, “For we have abandoned the land because our dwellings have been torn down.” (Jeremiah 9:19). The text says it plainly, and it isn't an easy line to read.

That's right, baker. The text says, “For death has climbed in through our windows; it has entered our fortresses…” (Jeremiah 9:21). Even the fortresses weren't shut to it. This is the reason the women are told to lament.
Famine is a heavy word, friend, but it isn't the one here. The text says death has climbed in through the windows and entered the fortresses (Jeremiah 9:21). This is the reason for the wailing.
Fire makes sense for a scorched land, baker. But the verse doesn't name it. It says death has climbed in through the windows and entered the fortresses (Jeremiah 9:21).

I wish it said that, friend. But the LORD says the corpses will fall like newly cut grain behind the reaper, “…with no one to gather it.” (Jeremiah 9:22). No one is there to gather them. That's a heavy line.

That's right, baker. The LORD says they will fall like newly cut grain behind the reaper, “…with no one to gather it.” (Jeremiah 9:22). This is one of the heavy parts of the passage, and the text doesn't soften it.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says, “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the wealthy man in his riches.” (Jeremiah 9:23). Wisdom, strength and riches are the three on the list. That's a whole pile of things people brag about.

Family, friend? I know a guy who can turn one cousin's promotion into a forty-minute speech, so I get the pull. But family didn't make this list. The LORD names the wise man in his wisdom, the strong man in his strength and the wealthy man in his riches (Jeremiah 9:23). Three men, three bragging rights, and not one of them is family. Nice swing, though!

Land is a reasonable guess, baker, since land and wealth often travel together. But the text doesn't name it. The third man is the wealthy man, and the LORD says not to boast in his riches (Jeremiah 9:23).

explanations.answer: That he understands and knows the LORD
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. The LORD says, “But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me…” (Jeremiah 9:24). So the boast isn't about what you've got. It's about knowing Him. Now THAT is worth bragging about.

explanations.answer: That he keeps every rule perfectly
explanations.explanation: That sounds impressive, friend, but it isn't what the LORD says. He says to boast “…that he understands and knows Me…” (Jeremiah 9:24). The boast is about knowing Him, not about a perfect record.

explanations.answer: That he gives more than his neighbors
explanations.explanation: Giving is a good thing, baker, but the LORD doesn't point to it here. He says to boast “…that he understands and knows Me…” (Jeremiah 9:24). Nobody has to win a contest with the neighbors.

I can see why that sounds possible, friend, but it's the other way around. The LORD says He exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth, “…for I delight in these things…” (Jeremiah 9:24). He doesn't just put up with them. He delights in them.

Yes, baker. The LORD says He exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth, “…for I delight in these things…” (Jeremiah 9:24). Not tolerates, delights. That tells you a lot about the One worth knowing.
That's right, baker. The list in the LORD's words is “Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab…” (Jeremiah 9:26). Judah is right there with the others. The text doesn't skip over its own people.
It does look surprising, friend. But the list says, “Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab…” (Jeremiah 9:26). Judah is named right along with the others, and the text doesn't leave it out.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, “…the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.” (Jeremiah 9:26). The problem He names for Israel is in the heart. That's a good reminder to keep checking in there.

Name is a fair guess, friend, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:26). Heart, not name. Easy to mix up when you're swinging fast, and I've done the same with a cookie tray.

SPEECH?! Baker, you swung at that blank like it owed you money, and I respect it. But that word isn't in the verse. The LORD says the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:26). Heart goes in the blank. Speech can sit this one out and cool on the rack.
